prompt.context: Your client, Melson, is a dominant (98% market share) manufacturer and seller of CT scanners in the US hospital market. The market is quite stable, and the U.S. demand for images from a CT scan grows 5% every year. At the beginning of last year, Melson launched a new CT scanner model that is sold at the same price but can produce 20% more images per year than the previous model. However, apart from the sales due to product replacement, the sales growth of the new model has been stagnant in the last year. The CEO has hired McKinsey to find out the reason for stagnant sales growth, and asked you how to increase sales.
prompt.question: Why has the sales growth of the new model been stagnant, and how can Melson increase sales?

clarifying_info.q: Does Melson sell any other products besides CT scanners?
clarifying_info.a: Melson only manufactures and sells one model at any time; when the new model goes to market, they stop manufacturing and selling old models.

clarifying_info.q: How long do the scanners last?
clarifying_info.a: The lifetime of both the old and new model are 8 years.

clarifying_info.q: How do hospitals decide how many scanners to buy?
clarifying_info.a: Hospitals match their number of scanners with image demand. There is no idle capacity; new purchases are driven by either replacement or increasing demand.
CT scanners produce images of patients for doctors to diagnose disease.

framework: Diagnose why new sales (beyond replacement) are stagnant: analyze demand growth vs. capacity supplied by new model
Quantify new incremental sales using demand = production equilibrium
Brainstorm levers to increase sales: price and volume
Formulate recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Q1: Why has the sales growth of the new model been stagnant?
questions.guidance: The key insight is that the new model produces 20% more images per scanner per year, but total image demand only grows 5% per year. Introducing a more efficient model reduces the total number of scanners needed to meet demand, so net new (non-replacement) sales are very low. A strong answer frames this as a supply-demand mismatch caused by the productivity improvement exceeding demand growth.

questions.prompt: Q2: What are the new sales of the new model (i.e., total sales excluding replacement sales)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up variables for the existing installed base and image output per scanner, then write a demand = production equation. The answer is that incremental new sales equal only 2% of the existing old-model scanner installed base. Strong candidates set up the algebra cleanly and interpret the result.

math.setup: Let X = total number of old-model scanners in all hospitals before new model launch. Let S = images produced per old-model scanner per year. New model produces 1.2S images per scanner per year. Scanner lifetime = 8 years, so annual replacement = X*(1/8). Let Y = new (non-replacement) sales of new model in year 1.
steps: Last year image production: from old models still in service = X*(7/8)*S; from replacement units (new model) = X*(1/8)*1.2S; from new sales = Y*1.2S
math.answer: New (non-replacement) sales of the new model ≈ 2% of the existing installed base of old-model scanners.

questions.prompt: Q3: How can Melson increase sales?
questions.guidance: This is a structured brainstorm. Strong candidates bucket ideas into price and volume levers, and within volume consider new segments, demand stimulation, and product strategy. Creativity is a bonus. Interviewer should keep pushing 'what else' until the candidate runs out.

brainstorming.prompt: How can Melson increase sales of its new CT scanner?

categories.name: Increase Price
ideas: Melson has a near-monopoly (98% market share) and the new model is superior; it can raise the price to capture more value per unit sold

categories.name: Increase Volume — New Segments
ideas: Sell to clinics and outpatient facilities (not just hospitals)

categories.name: Increase Volume — Product Strategy
ideas: Focus future R&D on image quality improvements rather than throughput, so hospitals do not need fewer scanners
Shorten the effective lifetime of scanners by dramatically improving quality so old models become obsolete and hospitals replace sooner

categories.name: Increase Volume — Demand Stimulation
ideas: Partner with media, healthcare associations, and key opinion leaders to educate patients and physicians that CT scanning is safe and early diagnosis saves lives, thereby growing total image demand
Improve marketing and sales force effectiveness

recommendation: Sales growth is stagnant because the new model is more productive (20% more images per scanner) while total demand only grows 5%, reducing the number of scanners hospitals need to purchase beyond replacement
Melson should increase the price of the new model — it is superior and the company holds a near-monopoly, so value capture through pricing is the most immediate lever
Melson should enter new customer segments (new geographies, research centers, clinics) to expand the addressable market
Melson should shift product roadmap toward image quality improvements rather than throughput gains to avoid further compressing its own replacement market
risks: A price increase may slow replacement rates if hospitals defer upgrades
Entering new segments requires investment and market development time
Competitor entry could be attracted by high margins if pricing is raised significantly
next_steps: Analyze price elasticity in the hospital segment to determine optimal price point for new model
Conduct market sizing for clinic and outpatient segments
Evaluate international market entry opportunities and regulatory requirements
Commission qualitative research on hospital CIO/CFO attitudes toward scanner replacement cycles
